bio:
architectural designer and environmental psychologist with six years of design practice and postgraduate training in the behavioural science of built environments. my work sits at the intersection of how people experience space and what that means for the environments we design, drawing on spatial literacy, qualitative research, and an understanding of how physical surroundings shape behaviour, wellbeing, and identity.

that intersection has a history to it. an undergraduate thesis first asked why some public spaces hold a hundred different stories while others hold only one, building a framework for how built form gets interpreted and imagined. a master's dissertation later returned to the same question with sharper tools, studying how physical space shapes the sense of identity people form in relation to it. the practice today carries that question forward: a building gets read before it gets used, and that reading shapes who a person becomes inside it.
